body_en:
I've never believed in the whole "deep state" thing. In ancient China, even a puppet emperor and a powerful minister could hardly coexist for long — let alone an emperor with real power. Claims like "the chaebol control Korea" or "the Jews control the American president" — take them with a grain of salt.

As House of Cards put it, power is a position: whoever sits on the throne is the emperor. If you don't step onto the stage, you can't really hold power. And whoever does sit in that seat will never give up what they've got. A fight like that is bound to play out in the open.

Take Trump, for one. Do you really think he's the kind of person who'd let someone stand behind him pulling strings? If you were the president of the United States — the most powerful person in the world — would you let a bunch of cockroaches and rats no one can see ride on your back?

If there really were a shadow government controlling the whole world, it would cost them more than just stepping into the open. Suppose Trump is your puppet — then every idea of yours has to go through Trump, in Trump's name. Here's the problem: if everything is done in Trump's name, then the people doing the work only answer to Trump. Who are you to give orders? Nobody would listen. Everyone knows Trump is your puppet — so how are you still hiding backstage? Take Maduro: he was your puppet, he followed your orders, but the American troops who came for him didn't know that. You'd get run over like a speed bump.

The biggest problem with a shadow government is that this system is the only thing that listens to you. Step outside that door, and you have no public standing, no status — nobody takes you seriously. One day a state trooper pulls you over on the highway — are you going to call Trump to get you out of it? Every single time? What if he doesn't pick up — are you not afraid of getting beaten with a baton, or shot for resisting arrest? If you're going to stay behind the curtain, you'd better be ready for one of your own underlings to accidentally kick you to death. Or else step onto the stage and let everyone know who you are. If nobody knows who you are, you have no power at all. You're a nobody. That's not a display of power — it's power castrated.

As Confucius said: "To govern is to set things right."

Why do so many people think that if the supreme ruler can't do whatever he wants, there must be a deep state — or that if a ruler's will is influenced by others, he's a puppet? Compromise is the norm of politics. Liu Bang didn't get his way on enfeoffing Yongchi, making Han Xin a king, or deposing and installing the crown prince. Li Shimin wanted to build Luoyang and go to Mount Tai for the Fengshan ceremony — one adviser after another talked him out of it, and none of it happened. Would you call Liu Bang a puppet? Would you say there was a deep state behind Li Shimin? No — that is precisely what makes them brilliant statesmen: they did the right thing, not the thing that felt good.

Interest groups certainly exist. Factions of all kinds within any organization are perfectly normal — a single dorm room can split into three or four group chats. That's human nature. Rulers even cultivate factions to set them against each other. The civil service forms interest blocs through blood ties, regional origins, and teacher-student bonds, and pushes hard for policies that benefit itself. If you want to call that a "deep state," I have no objection — but it is definitely not the "deep state" of Currency Wars. The difference is the master-servant relationship: whether it's the civil service or an interest group, they are sharing the emperor's power. They are the fox that walks ahead of the tiger, and the ghost that trails behind it.
excerpt_en: I don't buy the "deep state" story. Power is a seat — if you're not sitting in it, you don't hold it. And anyone who does sit in it will never give it up.
title_en: There Is No "Deep State" — and No One "Controls America"
